## 2026-11-03 — palette row: one defect in two halves, and the lever that follows

`0x46C5A0` keeps 376 of 6080 with object 6072 and no window closed, but the pass explains the whole shape of the failure and
leaves a specific lever. The gap trace reports 1884 reference instructions against 1913 object ones with both code ends equal
at 0x17c0, 526 events and 229 drift windows whose largest constant-drift span is only six instructions, so the streams are
misaligned from instruction four onward and no window is independently addressable. The first divergence is at offset 12,
native pushing esi where this build pushes ebx, and the register-aware diff reports 41 exact, 3 relocation, 59 register and
1806 structural of 1909.
The layout defect is proven from the native bytes: the reference has six arrays packed in declaration order totalling 0x680,
a buffer at minus 0x178, one at minus 0x1f8, a separate sprintf scratch at minus 0x2f8, and buffers at minus 0x3f8, minus
0x5f8 and minus 0x6f8, while this source has five arrays totalling 0x688. All three sprintf sites in the reference target the
0x100 scratch at minus 0x2f8 and none targets the 0x200 buffer, which only ever receives a copy of the first array, so 0x100
is its true extent. Applying the corrected sizes moves the frame from 0x6f8 to 0x6f0, moves the first mismatch to offset 5,
and costs one matched byte, so the sizing repair alone cannot pay.
The remaining eight bytes are explained: the reference's two memsets use the alignment-aware expansion, which spills the
destination and size to compiler temporaries at minus 0x24 and minus 0x20, while this build picks the fast expansion with
`rep stosd` and no temporaries. Those eight bytes of temporaries are exactly the difference between the reference's 0x78 and
this build's 0x70 scalar block, which is why the reference's palette local sits at minus 0x58 against minus 0x50 here and why
every array is eight bytes higher. Promoting the two values to function scope or marking them volatile both failed to produce
the homes, at 375 with frame 0x6f0 and at 331 with object 6204 and frame 0x6f4, because this compiler only homes a value that
its own inline memset or memcpy spills.
The root cause is therefore one defect in two halves. The register plan is a full permutation, with the reference using esi 145,
edi 228 and ebx 159 times against 219, 194 and 107 here, and the reference's extra spills are what give its blocks the register
plan it has. The recommended next step is to reach the memset destination through a pointer local so the alignment-aware
expansion and its two temporaries appear, and to apply the proven six-array layout in the same change rather than before it.
All seventeen direct callees resolve; the thirty-four unresolved bindings are CRT inlines, string literals, five globals and
local labels. Working notes, the native listing, the gap trace and the slot and drift helpers are in .scratch/0046c5a0/.

never appeared: computing the text base into an integer local leaves the prologue identical; taking the address of one local in the
cold early return produces the reference extent of 0x3200 with the text buffer at 0x260, but the match falls to 565 and the object
grows to 7659; taking the address of two cold-path locals gives 620 at 7543 with 200 windows; a double local for the two variadic
double pushes reproduces the reference's `fld` and `fstp` at both sites, which explains that sequence, but leaves the frame
unchanged and costs fifty matched bytes; sixteen integer locals in one ordered struct gives 601 at 7579; and splitting a reused
local in one case gives 606 at 7503. Every shape keeps two callee-saved pushes with the base at esp+8 and the immediate at 0x31f0.
The invariant that organises the whole row is now explicit and holds on both sides: the frame immediate plus four times the number
of callee-saved pushes equals the text buffer offset plus 0x2fa0. Here that is 0x31f0 plus eight, which is 0x31f8, and 0x258 plus
0x2fa0, the same number; in the reference it is 0x31f4 plus twelve, which is 0x3200, and 0x260 plus 0x2fa0. Two of the shapes
already reach the reference extent of 0x3200, so the reference immediate at 0x31f4 follows automatically from a third push and is
not separately reachable. The single missing fact is the third callee-saved register, with the reference keeping the text index in
ebx and a reused local in esi where this build keeps the index in esi and spills the local.
One diagnostic is recorded as a trap rather than a result: compiling at /O1 does reproduce the reference's x87 form and drops the
window count to 51 with a match of 796, but the object shrinks to 6544, so it is a false realignment rather than the right flags,
and the row's own flag set stays as configured.

being the second call of the grammar-state-zero if and else. This compiler if-converts the pair because the pointer lives in esi
here while the reference keeps it at [esp+0x20] with the kind at [esp+0x24] and the length in esi, and this build has the kind at
0x20 and the length in edi.

times into scratch registers.

## 2026-11-03 — palette row: the scalar block is declaration order in the reference, live range here

`0x46C5A0` keeps 440 of 6108 with the first divergence at offset 12 and an unchanged source, and the scalar permutation is now
mapped exactly rather than approximately. The reference's zero stores sit at minus 8 for the image index, minus 0x28 for the
extra-length flag, minus 0x64 for a loop flag, minus 0x18 for the line count, minus 0x1c for the colour and minus 0x60 for
another flag, each confirmed through that slot's later uses: the image index is read with `mov ecx,[ebp-8]` then indexed into a
table and incremented later, the extra flag guards three separate blocks as well as being stored and recomputed, the line count
feeds two indexed uses, and the colour receives four different immediate stores. This build keeps the same six values at minus 8,
minus 0x24, minus 0x64, minus 0x20, minus 0x18 and minus 0x60.
The decisive observation is structural: the reference's scalar block is exactly contiguous declaration order from the first
integer at minus 4 through the last locals, while this build packs by live range, with several names sharing one slot and two pairs
of locals transposed. That means the six zero stores are a symptom of the packing policy, not a reachable cause.
Every lever was measured with a compiler listing and disassembly. Six declaration permutations, including a full reverse and the
declaration-initialiser form, leave both the slot map and the frame byte-identical. Initialiser permutations change the store
order but not the slots. Volatile pins do move slots, with one local giving five of the six reference offsets and the line count
still at minus 0x20, but the best of them measures 446 at 6120 with the divergence still at 12, so it is worse and was rejected.
An ordered scalar structure holding twenty-four members in reverse order puts the block at minus 0x7c and shifts all six arrays by
0x10, breaking the frame. Compiling at a size or processor variant is not available under the translation unit's own flags.
The cause of the divergence at offset 12 is therefore register-home competition, with the reference keeping the zero in edi and the
slot in esi while this build keeps the zero in esi and the slot in ebx. That competition is upstream of the slot map, so no store
order or declaration change can reach it.

## 2026-11-03 — genitive row: the save premise was false, and the bodies differ per site

The save-placement task on `0x517C00` came back negative, and it corrects the premise it was given. No callee-saved value is live
across the dispatch: the only value live there is the pointer in esi, the destination stays in memory and is reloaded inside each case,
and both other registers first appear inside case 3, where ebx receives a computed address and ebp receives a table pointer. The eight
byte frame difference reported by the stack diagnostic is exactly the two extra saves rather than any local. Measured on reduced
copies with the same compiler, one case region using those registers defers the saves into the switch, two or three case regions that
are not disjoint still defer them, but case sets that include two specific cases hoist all four saves to function entry, so this
compiler's placement is controlled by how many disjoint regions use the registers and not by any source shape. Fifteen flag variants,
including processor and optimisation families, changed nothing, and the plain service-pack toolchain gave a different text size with
entry saves as well.
The bodies are also not identical modulo the shift, contrary to what an earlier entry claimed. Case 1's third test is a six-byte
compare in this build against a five-byte byte comparison in the reference, while cases 3 and 4 in the reference do use the six-byte
form, so the expression differs per site rather than being uniform. Case 3 schedules differently, with this build hoisting a load and
using a register test where the reference compares memory and reloads per branch. And a pre-switch return tail-merges into a far
shared epilogue with a six-byte jump where the reference has a local two-byte jump, worth four bytes. The next pass should decide
between the multi-region save-insertion problem and re-deriving the source from these per-site differences; three shapes that tried
the second direction measured 297 at 2804, 390 at 2736 and unchanged respectively.

## 2026-11-03 — d2 two: the blocker is where the thirteenth slot lands

`0x4DCF50` keeps 2345 of 8798 with frame 0x760 and an unchanged source, and the attempt to fit the native head order with a four-byte
give-back came back negative with a sharper explanation than the row had. The frame total is not the obstacle: the position of the
thirteenth stack slot is. The committed baseline has twelve live words from V 0x10 to 0x3c with the pointer's home at 0x18, the
message at 0x40, the table at 0xb0 and the record at 0x240, which reproduces every native aggregate base at frame 0x760. Adding the
native head initialisations makes thirteen live values, and the thirteenth, the pointer's home, lands between the message and the table
at V 0xb0, pushing the table to 0xb4 and the record to 0x244, so the whole aggregate block shifts by four bytes regardless of the frame
total. Shrinking a buffer therefore cannot move that word, and no aggregate is oversized: every baseline aggregate base already equals
the native one, and the only slot-freeing move is dropping the didFolter head store, which removes a native initialisation and is not
admissible.
Measured shapes, each built and restored: the baseline at 2345 with frame 0x760; the native head at 1617 with frame 0x764; the native
head without the later redundant float zeroing at 1689; that shape plus removing an unused padding local at 1887, the best native-head
result; the native head without the didFolter store at 1635 with frame 0x760 and the first twenty-one bytes matching native exactly;
and the best native-head shape plus a smaller buffer at 1888 but with the first fault moving from offset two to offset ten because the
record base is 0x244 against the native 0x240. Three give-back classes were eliminated by inspection: no aggregate is oversized, the
message structure has no usable padding member and the record and table only carry the rounding bytes of a 45-byte copy, and scalar
live-range work does not free a slot. The pointer never receives a register here because ebx is reused as a loop counter in the
selection fill, the filter, the float accumulation and the copy loops, so freeing it needs those loop shapes changed rather than a frame
give-back.

## 2026-11-03 — the row picker was parsing the store wrongly

The mis-picks above have a mechanical cause, and it is mine. The throwaway picker read the functions store with a record pattern that
did not match the file's actual headers, so it never opened a record at all and instead accumulated keys across unrelated lines. That is
why rows looked unbound, why sizes were stale values taken from history blocks, and why a GOLD row could appear in a GoldTL list: the
tool was reporting whatever the last stray key happened to say. After fixing the pattern to the real header form and requiring a bound
file, a size-mismatch or stub status, the GoldTL module and an inventory entry start, the picker reports 988 workable rows, and the
first entries are the rows this session has already been working, so its output is now consistent with what the store says.
Two stale-metadata facts were also confirmed while checking one pick: `0x4e2b70` has an inventory extent of 1199 rather than the 1733
recorded against a pre-correction snapshot, and it already has a bound source whose body measures 588 of 1270 against that 1199
reference, so it is an in-progress reconstruction rather than a missing one. Its stored blocker text likewise still quotes 1212 against
1199 while the object is 1270. The lesson applied from here: a row is only handed out after the picker confirms its status, module,
bound file and inventory presence, and the numbers in a brief come from that fresh read rather than from a record written earlier.

A row pass noticed that the address 0x100b0ac is referenced thirty times in the project but has no data row: the neighbouring row at 0x100b0a8 is four bytes and
the next row starts at 0x100b0c0, so the address falls in an unowned gap and every reference showed as an unresolved relocation.
The evidence for its extent and type is in the sources that use it: one function declares it as an integer and loops a count up to it three times, another
compares it against zero, and a third writes zero to it through an integer pointer. A data row was created through the metadata CLI at that address, four
bytes, typed as an integer, named as its users already name it, with object storage, guarded by the reviewed digest. The lint passes with no errors
afterwards.

## 2026-11-03 — the coordinate type layout claim is refuted, header untouched

A pass was opened to repair a declared layout in src/client_types.h on the strength of two readers that take a word at offset four and dwords at six and ten.
The evidence refutes the claim and the header was not changed. The declared layout is four-byte, four-byte, four-byte and a two-byte member at 0xc inside a
packed region, giving a size of fourteen, and a probe translation unit compiled with the project compiler confirms both the size and every member offset with
compile-time assertions. The two readers the claim rested on do not read through this type at all: one uses a ten-byte prefix of a different source type and
its row is EXACT at 58 bytes, while the other and a third helper use a clock view declared separately in their own rows, of which one is EXACT at 111 bytes and
one is a size mismatch at 145 against 147.
What does read through the type requires the declared layout. One row stores packet fields from the first, second and third four-byte members and a two-byte
member at 0xc, and a probe compiled with each candidate layout shows the reference matching the declared layout and not the clock layout; that row is a RELOC
at 715 of 715. Another row's block copies are layout-neutral because this compiler copies fourteen bytes as three dwords and a word under either layout, which
two more RELOC rows and one EXACT row demonstrate. The stride of fourteen is established by two rows that copy the value into calendar slots fourteen bytes
apart, one of them EXACT.
The type store has no binding for this type, so nothing needed refreshing, and the data row that names the object was left alone. Nine rows were re-measured to
show they are unchanged, covering three RELOC rows at full length, three EXACT rows and two size mismatches. The conclusion recorded for the future is that an
offset reading from a function only constrains the type that function actually uses, and overlapping views of the same bytes are separate types rather than
evidence of a single wrong declaration.

## 2026-11-03 — clock helper: one allocation explains both the overrun and the mismatch

`0x500BB0` keeps 30 of 147 with the object at 147 against a 145-byte extent, and the pass settles that the two-byte overrun and the poor match are one defect:
the reference build allocated a second callee-saved register for the minute accumulator, pushing edi and keeping the constant sixty in esi across both
divisions, while this build does not push edi, reuses esi for the accumulator and re-emits the constant before the second division. The byte arithmetic is
exact: one push and one pop per branch is three bytes short, the re-emitted constant is five bytes, and the net is the two-byte overrun, which the stack
diagnostic states directly as a frame of 0x8 against 0x4. Every instruction difference follows from that allocation, including the hoisted load of the minute
accumulator over the first division and the order of the two stores after the addition.
No type or call defect exists in the row: the field offsets and widths match, the zero extension is reproduced, the argument slots match, the function has no
calls, and both comparisons are signed. A type-permutation sweep of five field spellings either leaves one push or changes the tail width. Nine flag variants
were tried and only two change the code, both worse. Two spellings do reach 145 bytes but score lower. Notably the aliasing pragma that was used to explain a
server twin does not transfer here: the pragma is inert in this function although a probe confirms it reaches the compiler.
One byte-neutral change was kept for consistency: the row's private packed clock structure was replaced by the project's working clock declaration, the one the
two EXACT siblings use, which compiles to an identical object. The row stays a size mismatch and the recommendation is that it needs an evidenced different
translation-unit flag context or compiler build rather than more source shapes.

from the reference bytes or from a callee's body. The function takes a second character parameter: the reference reads a byte from the second argument slot

Two experiments were rejected: a fabricated pad that forced the reference frame moved the first divergence by six bytes only, and two memset spellings did not

## 2026-11-03 — zone row: two wrong call targets and a wrong counter field

`0x47F6B0` keeps 506 of 3193 with the object at 3129 and 32 relocations, and the pass found defects rather than shapes. Two direct call targets were wrong. The
first called an address that is not a function start at all, being mid-instruction, where the reference calls a different address whose relocation now validates
against the native value. The second called a three-argument zone lookup where the reference calls a one-argument plant-info routine, and the result's uses match
that routine's structure, with an identifier word, a name word and a byte at offset 0x42; the bound address now equals the reference target.
A counter was being kept in the wrong field of the state record: the reference increments the available count, compares the wanted count against it and stores it
to a global, and only later zeroes the total and the sent count, where the source used the total for all of it; the four uses are corrected and the tail stores
reordered to the reference's order. Two conditions were rewritten to the shapes the reference emits, a byte test followed by an unsigned jump rather than a zero
test, and a strict comparison replaced by an inclusive one. A duplicated call in the scan loop was removed where the reference calls once and loops. And a cached
pointer was left cached only in the loop that needed it, with its assignment moved after four setup calls so the first load lands where the reference's does.
That last repair partially inlined the pointer, and the full inline was measured: it reaches a structural ratio of 0.9658 but grows the object past the extent and
drops the match, so only the partial form was kept.
The positional count falls from 683 to 506 while the structural ratio reaches 0.8975 and several of the largest windows close, including three of 92, 84 and 35
bytes and two more at 26 and 14. The drop comes from the object being 64 bytes short, and the negative gaps around the scan block show this build's code is
condensed relative to the reference there, which is recorded as a shortfall rather than a regression. Every other checked class came back clean: push counts and
widths at every call site, both variadic argument counts, five strides, both bounds, the copy count, the argument orders at two calls, and the guards.

## 2026-11-03 — the row picker was hiding rows, and the frontier is not empty

A read-only pass across the untouched rows corrected two beliefs about what work remains. The picker had a bug: it recorded a row's address in its de-duplication
set before checking the module, so any GOLDTL row whose address is also used by a GOLD row was dropped from the list while the GOLD row consumed the address. The
fix is to check the module first and only then de-duplicate, which raises the workable set from 986 to 1010 and reveals 24 hidden rows. The largest hidden row is
0x42bf20 with an extent of 5840 bytes, whose file attempts the whole body and measures 1232 matched bytes, so it is the largest single unmatched span known.
The pass also tested twelve picker candidates and ranked them by extent minus matched bytes, which is the amount of unmatched code they represent. Four rows have
objects far below their extent, meaning a lead scaffold or a partial transcription rather than a body: 0x5c3f10 at 583 of 2768, 0x511c60 at 131 of 2577,
0x557460 at 925 of 2532 and 0x55f300 at 608 of 2504. The rest sit at or near their extent, which means their files already attempt the whole body and a pass on
them is repair rather than reconstruction.
Two further facts are recorded so later passes do not misread the store: a generic blocker line means no session has recorded work, not that the row is untouched,
since files under those rows contain real bodies; and the twelve untested candidates above 2700 bytes remain the frontier, from 0x5a59d0 at 2962 down to
0x5186c0 at 2756.

## 2026-11-03 — form row: one byte from a full match

`0x5373E0` moves from 2676 to 3070 matched bytes and from SIZE_MISMATCH to NEAR_MATCHING, with the object exactly at the 3071-byte extent and a single mismatched

stores into another and passes the first at the call, so the destination is corrected and the call's argument pair now matches. The loop condition re-read the
destination where the reference tests the byte it just loaded from the source, which the rewritten condition reproduces byte for byte. A global that the reference

than a proven semantic defect, since it changes which of two behaviourally equivalent readings the compiler emits.
The remaining byte is an opcode choice: the reference uses a sign jump where this build uses a less-than jump after a test, which sets the overflow flag to zero
so the two are equivalent. Seven spellings were tried for it and all were rejected, including negations, unsigned casts, a signed char cast and a plain
non-volatile reread, which regressed the row. Fifteen other defect classes were checked and the rest came back clean: every call relocation validates, the
cleanup matches, the frame matches at 576, the sentinel store matches, and no wrong stride, guard, duplicated scan, hoisted conversion, pointer read or record

## 2026-11-03 — eighty lead pads removed, and what that changes

Eighty GoldTL row sources carried a lead pad: a `_tlead_` byte array of 0x90 filled into a data segment named as text, placed ahead of the bound function. Every one
compiled into its own text section before the function, which is why the gap diagnostic described padding instead of code on the rows this session had already found
by hand. All eighty were removed, 70,432 bytes of text pads in total, and the object's text section now starts at the function in every case.
The evidence that they were not original content: each is a run of 0x90 with a comment saying it is not reconstruction, and the link map shows the pad occupying the
row's own address while the function lands later, with the matched byte count and the function's object size unchanged before and after in all eighty rows. The gap
diagnostic now leads with real instructions on the rows that were named in the audit, 0x44fc70, 0x44b480 and 0x4079f0 among them, and its first fault is the frame
or slot difference that the row is actually blocked on.
Two consequences are recorded rather than left to be discovered. The raw link layout is now stale by the removed amount, since the pads were shifting objects
forward, so any link-based placement measurement must be re-taken before it is trusted. And the script that writes these pads, scripts/gen_text_lead.py, sizes a
filler from each object's deficit against the link map; running it again would recreate the pads and the diagnostic defect, so it must not be run on this tree as
it stands. Removing the pads does not change any object's match count, and it makes the pad rows' measurements describe the function for the first time.
Removal was by copying scratch backups, not by version control. The twenty-six files that carry the empty scaffold comment and pragma with no array were left
alone, as were two `_dpad_` arrays in 0x448360 and 0x457630, which are tentative data definitions rather than text fillers. Lint passes with no errors.

## 2026-11-03 — the gap diagnostic now picks the function's own text section, fixed upstream

The defect this session hit on four rows is fixed in the upstream checkout with a regression test rather than worked around here. The gap diagnostic took the
first text section of the compiled object, which is wrong whenever a translation unit emits more than one: a lead pad or filler becomes a section of its own
ahead of the body, so the trace described padding and every window it reported was meaningless. The helper now counts the function symbols each text section
defines and decodes the section that defines the most, falling back to the first text section when none defines any, which keeps the old behaviour for ordinary
objects that have a single section. Two tests cover both paths with a synthetic object: one where a pad section precedes the function's section, and one where
no section defines functions.
Verified against the live tree: on the row that carried a 3008-byte lead pad the diagnostic previously reported the pad's instructions and a NOP as the first
fault, and it now reports 873 object instructions ending at 0xaf0 with a push as the first event, which is the real body. The project environment was
reinstalled from the checkout so the fix is what runs here, and the upstream commit is ef93c5a1 with the affected test file and the type check passing.

## 2026-11-03 — the frame diagnostic note is corrected: it reports peak depth

The note filed two entries ago is wrong and is corrected here. The frame diagnostic was reported as disagreeing with the object's prologue on row 0x00595330, and the
gap trace's section-selection bug was blamed. The diagnosis refutes that. The stack path already resolves the object bytes through the symbol table and slices from
the function's own section, so it never took the first text section; the object in question has a single text section anyway, and both diagnostics see the same
bytes starting with the same frame adjustment.
The real cause is the metric: the frame analysis returns peak stack depth, which its own docstring and an existing test confirm, and the depth model does not credit
argument pushes back after a call while assuming that stdcall callees pop their arguments. On this row both prologues are identical, each subtracting 0xf0 and
pushing four registers for a peak of 0x100, and the reported eight-byte difference is the instruction stream's divergence amplified by that model. The fix, if one
is wanted, is to report the local frame by crediting arguments at each call, which changes existing expectations and touches the near-analysis caller, so it belongs
in its own change with updated tests. The upstream note was rewritten to describe this rather than the imagined section bug.

## 2026-11-03 — an over-merged-row scan, and why a linear sweep cannot decide it

Because one row this session turned out to cover three functions and became a full relocation match once split, every inventory row was scanned for the same defect: a
second function prologue inside a row's extent, preceded by a return or a jump and not itself a branch target. Readings outside the same binary's library band were
listed, and each candidate in the game band was checked by disassembling at the reported offset.
That check refuted the list. Disassembling at three GOLD candidates gives misaligned instruction text, which means the reported offsets are not instruction boundaries.
The cause is the method, not the rows: a linear disassembly from the row start desynchronises when a row contains an inline jump table or a constant pool, which many
game rows do, so every byte after the table is decoded at the wrong boundary and spurious prologues appear. The one real case this session was found by reading the
transition between two functions directly, where the second starts with its own stack adjustment and two pushes and the boundary is unambiguous.
So the conclusion recorded here is a method limit rather than a clean bill: no over-merged game row is known beyond the one that was split, and a reliable scan needs
control-flow-aware decoding that starts from each row's entry and follows branches, ignoring bytes that no path reaches. The scratch script that produced the candidate
list is kept with that caveat and must not be treated as evidence without disassembling each hit at its own boundary.

## 2026-11-03 — a compiler hash changed under the rows, and what it means

Five row records now carry a different compiler hash than they did, and the cause is tooling rather than source: the project environment runs Rebrew from the local
checkout so the fixes made in this session are in effect, and the recorded hash reflects that environment. The bytes measured are unchanged; the hash is provenance,
and it is the honest record that these verdicts were taken with the development tooling rather than the released wheel.
The consequence for the goal is stated plainly rather than buried: reproducing these rows from a clean environment requires either installing the same checkout or
releasing the upstream fixes, and until one of those happens the stored hashes will differ on a released wheel even where the object bytes agree. That is the pending
release note already recorded for this session, and this entry is the same fact from the metadata side.

## 2026-11-03 — physics row: a prefix-only row transcribed into its body

`0x52C060` had 170 bytes of object code and 57 matching bytes; it now has 2331 bytes and 580 matching bytes, with 553 instructions against the reference's 572 and the
object's code end ninety-six bytes short of the reference's.
The row was prefix-only, so the work was transcription rather than defect repair. The body now covers the prologue with its 0x90 frame, the early gates and state restore,
the first physics block, the one-shot update block, and the matrix and sine-cosine prediction tail. The layout is three vector pairs, a rotation vector, a position vector
and a sixteen-float matrix at 0x60, which is what makes the frame match. Two pairs of globals are declared as sixteen-bit because the reference reads them with a
sign-extending word load. The entity table stride is 0x21c. Seven callee conventions and arities were derived from the callees themselves, including a two-argument
stdcall, a two-argument cdecl returning a float, and a three-argument cdecl.
Two variants were reverted: a position vector typed wrongly, which shrank the frame, and a declaration swap that gained nothing. The first remaining divergence is
callee-saved register assignment, where the reference holds three constants in three registers and this build assigns the same three to different registers, so every
block offset after the prologue shifts; no convention, operand or precision defect remains identified.

## 2026-11-03 — request row: a loop compared the wrong operand, and a local that fixes the frame

`0x487F90` moves from 196 to 297 matched bytes with the frame now exactly 0x100, matching the reference at 292 bytes and the same two slot offsets. The object is 2368
bytes against the 2309 extent, so it is over by fifty-nine, where the baseline was thirty-eight over and shorter.
Three repairs were kept. A scan loop compared a request field against a base pointer where the reference compares the count it reloaded from a slot, which is worth
sixty-seven matched bytes. A forty-entry free-record scan tested the flag first where the reference tests the bound at the top and the flag at the bottom, so the
condition order is swapped, worth another thirty-four. And one pointer local was added so the frame grows to the reference size, which by itself moved no matched bytes
but aligned every stack displacement.
Two leads from an earlier row were confirmed rather than assumed: the request really is 0x24 bytes with nine fields at multiples of four, and the record field offset of
0x16c is right. All seven callees match in push count and argument order, and the globals are at their reference widths.
Two defects are found and not fixed, both labelled. The reference shares one call-and-return tail across five source tails, reached by a jump, where this build emits five
separate tails; that is the same codegen behaviour already documented for other rows and it accounts for about thirty of the fifty-nine excess bytes. And the four walks
over a 0x21c stride address the same bytes from a different anchor, which costs an extra address computation per iteration without changing what is read.

## 2026-11-03 — the displaced data symbol: cause found, one duplicate pad removed, and a measurement caveat

The action list's largest item was a 589,824-byte data symbol reported as displaced. The extent is not the defect: the header declares a 768 by 768 byte matrix and
every use indexes it that way, so 0x300 times 0x300 is the reference extent. The displacement decomposes exactly on the current tree into three parts. Initialised data
is 0x63534 bytes where the reference raw section is 0x40FC0, an excess of 140,660 caused by initialised pad declarations sized against an older metadata set that now
cover rows that have definitions of their own. The .bss side is short by 37,824 because the symbol is defined in a generated stub translation unit and the stub packs it
next to its neighbours, while every one of the 273 BSS pads in this tree is a tentative definition that the compiler emits as a common symbol, so the linker appends it
at the end of the section and a pad cannot hold a reference gap at all. The remaining 53,248 bytes are section layout, from text and read-only data sizes, not data
declarations.
One defect in this tree was fixed and measured. A translation unit declared the same reference bytes twice with two pads whose initialisers are byte-identical over the
overlapping span; the second declaration was removed, so the same bytes are still emitted once. A rebuild and relink of that unit takes initialised data from 0x63534 to
0x5C8B4, the displaced symbol from 0x88f640 to 0x8889c0, and the second largest displaced symbol from 0x91f650 to 0x9189d0, and the row's function still measures a
full relocation match at 808 of 808 with 49 relocations.
Two things are recorded as not established. Removing the remaining 112,884 bytes of over-allocation needs the stale pads reconciled or regenerated from current metadata
and then relinked, and the padding fill command skips existing pad names, so the pads have to be removed first. And holding a gap inside the bottom of the data section
needs real owner translation units for those globals rather than common declarations, which the reference does not tell us because it carries no link map.
A measurement caveat is recorded with the change: the required data verification ran against a build image from before this session's pad split, so it rewrote 1,260
verification blocks in the data store with measurements from that stale image, including status changes. Those blocks are tool-written measurements, not hand edits, and
they must be refreshed by re-running the verification after a fresh link.

`0x480330` moves from 179 to 294 matched bytes with the object at 2321, inside the 2340 extent, and the frame now matches at 0x50c with the message buffer at 0x14 and

frame size is reached, which is labelled as a codegen device rather than proved original source, and it costs three memory accesses.

## 2026-11-03 — the message row's whole-row blocker: a macro that weights its own argument

`0x569FF0` keeps 976 of 3772 with the object four bytes short and the frame matching at 0x738, and no change was kept, but the pass located the blocker that explains the
row. A message-copy macro in that file expands its destination argument four times, which raises the parameter's allocation weight enough that the compiler keeps the
parameter in one callee-saved register for the entire function where the reference keeps it in another. Everything downstream is register-permuted, which is why the row
shows 169 replace events and a head window of 909 bytes.
The reference's own expansion computes the destination once and stores through it, and rewriting the macro that way flips the parameter into the reference's register and
makes the first sixteen bytes identical. Doing that alone exposes a four-byte frame shortfall, because the reference keeps one value in a local that the source does not
have: at entry it zeroes three separate registers with four zero stores where the fixed build uses one. The pass measured the macro variants as structurally closer but
650 matched bytes worse, and reverted them rather than trade position for structure without the missing local, which is the right call; the two changes have to land
together and that is what the next pass is asked to do.
A float wording is also recorded as disproved: the value near the first stack slot is a four-byte float, since the reference loads a dword, multiplies by a quadword
constant and stores a dword back, and the flag beside it is separate. A variant that declared it double was reverted on that evidence.
One brief mistake is recorded too: the task statement quoted an extent of 2273 where the store and the inventory both say 3772, which the reading agent caught before
editing. Addresses and sizes belong to the tool outputs, not to memory, and the brief for a row must be built from the record rather than typed.

all 169 initialised pads whose encoded address falls in the reference raw region match the reference image byte for byte at that address, so the pads are reference
content rather than waste. The rule overstated the problem by an order of magnitude, and that correction is recorded because it changes what the remaining excess means.

falls from 0x5C8B4 to 0x56AB4, which is 354,996 bytes against the reference 0x40FC0, so the excess falls from 112,884 to 88,820. The two displaced symbols improve with it:
the large matrix moves from 0x8889C0 to 0x882BD8 and the second one from 0x9189D0 to 0x912BE8. One intermediate step caused a data row to go from verified to drifting
because a split moved the initialised spill boundary onto a reference BSS byte; the next step that removed another 320 bytes put it back, and the final state has the same
four drifting rows as the baseline and eight verified, with no layout violations and a clean lint.
What remains is blocked rather than skipped, and the reason is stated: the eighteen pads the flat audit still flags hold only 1,766 bytes covered by an emitted
definition; the rest of each is reference content that nothing else emits, and splitting around the duplicated bytes would cost a thirty-two-byte piece per uncovered run,
so the final plan over 160 pads has nothing left to shrink and would grow initialised data by 10,592. Attributing the remaining bytes needs a reference link map or
reference data extents for objects whose symbols do not encode a reference address, and neither exists in this tree.
The data store's verification blocks were refreshed against the fresh link from this pass, which supersedes the stale-image measurements recorded earlier.

Verifying data against the fresh link from the pad pass reports 768 rows matching, and the store counts eight verified and four drifting rows, but the status summary

## 2026-11-03 — the message row's copy macro now computes its destination once

The message-copy macro expanded its destination argument four times, so the parameter it names carried four times the weight in allocation and the compiler kept it
in a register the reference does not use. The macro now takes the address once and stores through it, which puts the parameter in the reference's register and drops three
relocations. The reference does exactly this at its own expansion sites, so the change is more faithful than what it replaces.
The cost is measured rather than hidden: matched bytes fall from 976 to 324 because the frame is four bytes short, which shifts every stack displacement, and the two
signals therefore disagree. The missing slot was searched for and not found. It is a reserved dead slot: the reference frame has a four-byte scalar slot that no
instruction in the 1,224-instruction body touches at any push depth. Six candidate initialisations were tried and none changed the frame or the zero-register count, and
two shapes that reserved the slot explicitly, a volatile integer and a pointer, produced the correct adjustment on neither side or were elided entirely.
The row is left at the faithful macro with both numbers recorded, because the previous state matched more bytes while allocating the parameter to a register the reference
never uses, and keeping that would mean keeping a wrong register home for a byte count. The next pass has to find what makes the compiler reserve a slot it never reads;
until then this row cannot convert its structural gain into bytes.

49 to 46.
Three repairs were kept. One branch wrote an item's key at a packet offset one field too high, leaving the real key slot zero so the first record found overwrote it;
the reference stores to the lower offset and then fills consecutive slots from that base, which is what proves the correct field. A loop's two conditions were in the
wrong order, which put one test at the loop top and the other at the latch, while the reference tests the pointer bound at the top and the index at the latch. And the
row's private entity structure is replaced by the shared entity type that uses the same 0x21c stride and identifier offset, which a sibling row already uses for the same
table; the output is byte-identical, so this is fidelity rather than a metric change.
A claim from my own notes was disproved and is recorded as such: I had read the reference's index chain and two stores as evidence that the key offsets were wrong, but
tracking the stack through the branch's push shows the stores land where the source already had them, the scale chain is the one the source uses, and the load is the
shared record's identifier field. So that part of the notes was wrong and no change was made for it.
The remaining divergence is where the compiler places a loop-header zero and how it cross-jumps branch tails: the reference cross-jumps one item's tail with another's,

## 2026-11-03 — event row placement: six missing masks were the gap, and the cross-jump pair will not move

`0x5B3B60` moves from 1146 to 1312 matched bytes with the object at 2291 against the 2293 extent, and two landmarks now land exactly on their reference offsets. The whole
gain comes from six call sites where the reference masks a random argument to sixteen bits after the call and the source passed the raw value, so six instructions were
missing and the branches after them sat early. Masking both arguments at those sites puts the fourth and sixth item branches at the reference offsets.
The placement question is answered negatively and that answer is the useful result. The compiler pairs the first and fourth item tails in this build where the reference
pairs the first and fourth differently: the reference gives the shared finish copy the accumulator form of the address computation and the first item the other register,
while this build gives the first item that form and the second item the shared one, exactly reversed. That single register choice decides which two tails merge. Nine
shapes were measured, including chain reorder, condition inversion, store reorder, hoisting and a dropped duplicate; none moved the pair, and the chain reorder proved the
compiler emits these branches in source order rather than reordering them. Two shapes are recorded as byte-identical no-ops rather than kept as changes.
One claim in the brief used to drive that pass was wrong and is corrected here: the reference does not test the items in a different order from the source. Its comparison
order is exactly the source's, and the machine code confirms the compiler does not reorder the chain. A switch is not expressible for this row either, because the
discriminators are runtime item handles rather than integer constants, and a switch would add a comparison chain before the switch and move the first divergence.
What remains is register allocation around the loop header and one reload inside a loop, not field offsets: the first divergence at reference 0x13a is a sunk zero on the
latch paths, and the last two bytes of drift are a register restored after the loop instead of inside it.

`0x56B700` moves from 153 to 499 matched bytes with the object at 2140 against the 2188 extent and the frame now exactly 0x158 where it began at 0x20c. The first
forty-two bytes are now identical to the reference where the baseline diverged at offset two.

the buffer base and the counted zeroing at the reference address. The position field was declared as three floats where the reference has a fourteen-byte structure, and

integer-to-float load, multiplies by the constant and converts in the floating-point register, where the old form pushed a float and called a conversion routine with an

reference. A mode-and-count test now emits two calls on one path and one call on the other, as the reference does. And a value saved before the switch was moved into the

## 2026-11-03 — a twenty-eight-byte row, and the tail call this compiler will not stop making

A rounding hunt began on the store's smallest size-mismatched rows because closing small ones is cheap and each one adds to the exact count. The smallest, `0x4DA170`, is
twenty-eight bytes and turned into a clean negative that says something about the compiler. The reference tests a global, jumps when it is set, and in the other arm
pushes its argument, calls one routine, adjusts the stack and returns, while the set path is a single jump to the other routine. This build instead emits a jump to each
routine from both arms, with no call, because both calls are in tail position and the optimiser converts them.
Five source shapes were measured: a call with a return, an if and else with a trailing return, the zero path first, a goto form with an out-of-line block, and a prototype
that returns an integer instead of nothing. All five produce the same two-jump object. A flag sweep is informative rather than a fix: with the frame pointer disabled the
object keeps the two jumps, and with the frame pointer enabled the calls become plain calls with a stack adjustment and a return, which is the shape the reference has,
but a frame pointer the reference does not have. So the reference's shape needs both an inlined call and no frame pointer, which this toolchain does not produce from any
spelling tried; that is a per-translation-unit flag question and needs evidence about the original unit before it can be applied, not a source edit.
Nothing was kept and the row is restored byte for byte. The sweep is recorded because a later pass with translation-unit evidence can use it directly, and because it
prevents the next session from repeating five dead ends.

another, and this build has the two exchanged, which propagates to a second exchange higher in the frame and to two register swaps. Seven declaration orders compiled to

another when written as less-or-equal, which makes the strictness of a float compare provable from the reference's own mask byte rather than inferred.

## 2026-11-03 — two-byte near miss: order solved, register not

A rounding pass over the store's nearest rows found a thirty-three-byte function that differs in exactly two bytes, both from one register choice. The reference loads a
global into edx after a call, stores a converted result to an absolute address, then stores zero through the pointer; this build loads it into ecx. Four source shapes
were measured. The baseline and one variant both keep the byte count at 31 of 33. Moving the pointer's assignment next to its use makes the instruction order identical to
the reference, load then the absolute store then the pointer store, but the register stays ecx. An explicit reload expression gets edx but puts the load after the
absolute store. A volatile pointer produced a spill and a stack store, which is worse.
So the two signals cannot both be satisfied from source here: the order and the register are chosen independently by the allocator, and no spelling tried gets both. The row
is restored byte for byte and the result is recorded, because two bytes on a thirty-three-byte row is not worth a shape that trades order for register; the lesson is that
near rows with a single register difference are as hard as large ones and should be scheduled after rows that are missing whole blocks.

## 2026-11-03 — near rows: two measured walls on thirty-two and thirty-three bytes

Two of the store's nearest rows were worked and both ended where they started, with the wall identified rather than guessed. On the thirty-three-byte function the only
difference is which register holds a reloaded global: making the instruction order match the reference keeps a different register, an explicit reload gets the reference's
register but moves the load after a store, and a volatile pointer spills to the stack. Order and register are chosen independently, so no spelling gets both.
On the thirty-two-byte counting loop the reference keeps the loop counter in one register and the loaded value in another, pushes a saved register, and orders its prologue
one way; this build assigns the two values to the opposite registers and orders the pushes differently. Four shapes were measured: a do-while, an endless loop with a
break, an unsigned counter, and a form with no intermediate value at all. The first three compile identically to the baseline, and dropping the intermediate produces a
shorter object that is further from the reference.
Both rows are restored byte for byte. The conclusion recorded for scheduling is that a near row differing only in register allocation is as expensive as a row missing
whole blocks, so future passes should prefer rows with missing code over rows with single-register deltas.

## 2026-11-03 — four near rows measured to their walls, and a fifth shape tried

Four more near rows were worked and none closed, each with its cause pinned to a compiler behaviour rather than a source defect. All sources are restored and match the
store's own hashes.
A seventy-four-byte row hoists an address computation before a global store and pushes it, where the reference stores first, computes the address, pushes it and then
finishes its buffer stores; a pointer local written for that purpose produced identical bytes, and the row already carried the same finding from an earlier pass. An
eighty-four-byte row differs in six bytes of address arithmetic: the reference shifts an index then adds a constant base, while this compiler reassociates the constant
into the index and shifts afterwards, which is algebraically the same and produces different bytes; that row also carries an older compiler hash in its record, so its
stored verdict came from the previous environment. An eighteen-byte-wide window in a one-hundred-and-eighteen-byte row is a single instruction pair the scheduler orders
differently, a compare before a move against a move before a compare, and the one shape that changed it regressed the branch layout instead. And the thirty-two-byte row's
register swap is confirmed again.
Two further shapes were tried here on the reassociation row and both produce identical bytes: separating the offset into its own local and adding the base there, and
advancing a typed pointer by the index so that scaling happens through pointer arithmetic. That makes six shapes on that row, all folded by the compiler, so the
reassociation is recorded as a wall rather than an open question.

## 2026-11-03 — near row closed: a pipelined load needs two alternating temporaries

`0x445EC0` closes from a near match to a relocation match at 135 of 135 with two validated relocations. The reference pipelines six global loads one ahead of their
stores: each load is issued before the previous value is stored, so the store order and the register that holds each value differ from a plain sequence. A source shape
with one cached temporary produces load, load, store, store and then strict pairs. Rewriting it with two alternating temporaries, assigning the second before the first
is stored, reproduces the reference byte for byte. That makes this a source-shapeable class rather than a wall, and it is recorded as a technique: when the reference
interleaves loads and stores, alternate two temporaries instead of caching one.
Three more near rows were measured to walls in the same pass. A one-hundred-and-ten-byte row is exactly 98 of 110 under the processor-pack profile, but the same source is
110 of 110 under the plain service-pack profile, and both images share the same compiler front end while the pack ships a different code generator; the translation unit
is genuinely pack-compiled elsewhere, since two sibling functions match fully under the pack and not under the plain profile, so a per-row override would be unjustified
and the row is a code-generator ordering wall. A one-hundred-and-twenty-one-byte row swaps two registers that the prologue saves in the other order, and five declaration
and initialisation shapes left it unchanged. A one-hundred-and-twenty-three-byte row places a copy-count move ten bytes from where the reference does, and six shapes were
worse or equal. A one-hundred-and-thirty-byte row rotates three registers, and six shapes did not move it.

## 2026-11-03 — correction: data verified bytes are zero because drift outranks verified, not because rows lack sizes

The earlier entry that blamed the zero byte count on data rows carrying no size is wrong and is corrected here. The rows have sizes: the large verified ones declare
thirty-six thousand and thirty-five thousand bytes and their computed sizes agree with the declarations, and the small ones declare one and four bytes. The accounting
instead buckets each byte once with a stated precedence, so a byte inside a drifting span is counted as drift and cannot also count as verified. The four verified rows in
this target are all overlapped by drifting rows, which is why four verified rows contribute nothing at byte level while the drift bucket carries what they cover.
That makes the number honest rather than broken: data verification reports the truth that almost every tracked data byte currently sits inside a drifting symbol, and the
way to change it is to fix placement, which is what the pad reconciliation began. It also means the earlier claim about writing sizes for twelve hundred rows was aimed at
the wrong problem and is withdrawn.

## 2026-11-03 — an attempt to find the text rows that inflate the built image, and why the method failed

With initialised data still a hundred thousand bytes past the reference and part of that caused by section layout, an attempt was made to find which functions inflate
the built `.text` by comparing each built symbol span from the link map against the stored reference extent. The first rows it ranked are impossible: a hundred-and-seventy
byte reference showing thirty-two thousand eight hundred built bytes, and a hundred-and-thirteen byte row showing thirty-one thousand. Those are not function bodies but
gaps and alignment between map symbols, so the span-from-next-symbol assumption does not hold in a link whose text has holes.
The method is therefore recorded as unreliable rather than acted on, and nothing was changed from it. A trustworthy version needs per-row object sizes from the compiler
rather than spans from addresses, which means a batch compile; that is a separate, deliberate run rather than something to infer from a map.

## 2026-11-03 — the constant hoist is not reachable from source, proved three ways

The lever recorded for `0x50EE80` was chased and closed. Four source shapes were tried and three of them compile to byte-identical text: division by one, per-arm

worse and still hoisted the constant at the same address. So the compiler reaches one constant node from every preserving spelling and folds it.

kept, still produces the hoisted move at function entry and still leaves the pointer out of the register the reference uses it for. That rules out use count and spelling:

register and leaves the second pointer with no home at all. The reference's own use of a register for the same constant sits inside one block, which is the same pass making
a block-local choice.

row needs a different approach than point editing: either the loop's shape has to change so the constant is not live across the back edge, or the row stays parked.

## 2026-11-03 — the gap window note is corrected: the symbol-spacing default is deliberate

The upstream note filed earlier said the gap diagnostic should prefer the reviewed extent. Reading the function that derives the window shows why it does not: a function with
an out-of-line jump table or case map is longer than its metadata size, and decoding only the metadata window turns table bytes into phantom instructions, which is the worse
failure. So the default is correct and preferring metadata outright is not proposed.
What remains worth asking for is a note: when the metadata size and the symbol-derived window differ, print both and say which the window came from. A caller who wants the
reviewed window can already pass the size explicitly, so the missing piece is visibility, not a different default. The upstream note is rewritten to that, and this replaces
the earlier version rather than adding a second entry.

`0x589930` was taken up because its object already equals its extent, so the difference is ordering rather than missing code. The reference converts a count to floating
point once and multiplies it by three constants, and the divergence is one instruction: it issues the multiply for the third conversion before storing the second result,
where this build stores first and multiplies after. Removing the cached float and writing each conversion inline as one expression changed nothing, because the compiler
already keeps the value in a register across the conversions; swapping the second and third assignments lowered the match from 596 to 591.
Both variants are reverted and the row stays at 596 of 990 with its object at the extent. The result is recorded because it is another instance of a pattern now seen
several times: when two independent conversions are in flight, the compiler's scheduling decides their interleaving and source order does not, so a row whose only remaining
difference is that interleaving should be parked rather than worked.

## 2026-11-03 — two shop rows: a bound that could not fold, and a ratio compared in the wrong width

flag byte where the reference writes the second; a record loop indexed one slot too high, which matches the identifier array it pairs with; both packet fill loops now stop

recorded rather than padded: the first zero-initialised slot is at a different frame offset with every other slot equal, and one case keeps an inline copy of a store-and-return
in the reference where this build cross-jumps to another case's copy.
The row now reports a stub verdict with its object exactly at the extent, while its frame, code end and instruction count are within three instructions of the reference.

## 2026-11-03 — the opposite tail merge: the reference repeats an epilogue this build shares

`0x57E0A0` was taken up because its object already equals its extent with 1029 of 1976 bytes matching, so the difference is ordering. The first three gates in the reference
each end with their own copy of the same epilogue: pop two registers, load minus four, pop the third, return. The source already writes three separate returns, and this build
merges them into one shared tail, so the object is fourteen instructions longer than the reference and every offset after the first gate drifts.
That is the reverse of the usual tail-merge wall: here the faithful shape is the duplicated one, and no source spelling forces a compiler to stop sharing an identical
epilogue. The row is parked with that evidence rather than worked further, because every window after the first gate is a consequence of it.

## 2026-11-03 — two addresses written from memory instead of read from the store, and how it surfaced

This round I wrote two row addresses into a delegation brief from memory rather than copying them from the store listing. Neither address exists in the function store, so
both delegated passes had nothing to compare against and stopped instead of touching a file. The check that caught it was cheap: looking the two keys up in the store before
the sessions could do work, which returned missing for both.
The rule this repeats is already in the ledger and was broken again: copy every address and every path verbatim from tool output, never reconstruct one. The replacement
briefs were built from a store scan that printed the address, the extent and the bound path together, and both of those addresses exist.

## 2026-11-03 — an invalid address left a row behind, and the tool cannot remove just that one

The two addresses I wrote from memory turned out to be interior addresses of existing functions, and one of the delegated passes ran the prescribed comparison anyway on a guess
at the owning file. That comparison wrote a row for the interior address with no file, symbol or name, and reported 45 of 240 matched against a window that starts
mid-instruction, so those numbers describe nothing. The pass was right to say so rather than report progress.
The row cannot be removed narrowly. Listing orphans finds it among 1342 entries, and pruning takes no selector, only a switch to include rows that carry earned verdicts, so
running it would remove far more history than the one mistaken row. The row is therefore left in place with status stub and no binding, which is inert, and the gap is filed
upstream: comparison should refuse an address that is not an entry start, and pruning should accept a selector so a single mistaken row can be removed.
This is the third time an address reconstructed rather than copied has cost a pass. The remedy is procedural and already in the ledger: take the address, extent and path from
one store scan and paste them together.

## 2026-11-03 — the venv was measuring with the released wheel, which crashes the gap diagnostic

A delegated pass reported that `rebrew diagnose gap` crashes on one row with a type error from the aligner, and that the local checkout already contains the repair while the
installed package does not. That was correct and it is the more important finding of the round: the project venv held the released 6.16.0 wheel rather than the checkout, so
every gap diagnostic run in this session executed the released code, which lacks the masked-key repair and the object-text section selection repair.
Two consequences. First, the crash is real on Python 3.15 for any translation unit whose disassembly yields a branch key, because capstone returns a bytearray and the released
helper returns a bytearray slice for branch keys, which the aligner cannot hash. Second, diagnostics on translation units that emit more than one text section were run against
the older selector, so any window list produced from a lead-padded unit in this session is suspect and should be recomputed rather than trusted.
The repair is upstream and now complete: the helper's signature admits a bytearray, the body returns bytes for every path, and a regression test covers all three key kinds.
The venv is reinstalled from the checkout in compat editable mode, which is the tooling-development opt-in the ledger already describes; the reproducible state is the released
wheel and returning to it is `uv sync` once no tooling repair is in flight.

## 2026-11-03 — two rows advanced: an inverted near-plane gate, and four locals the reference zeroes at entry

`0x45A9D0` moves from 127 to 148 matched bytes with the object from 1542 to 1820 against the 2040 extent. The body was rebuilt to the native shape and the repairs are semantic:
a near-plane gate was inverted, including which side sets the split flag and that the split picks its neighbours from a minimum or maximum vertex chosen by comparing two
absolute differences rather than always the maximum; the copy of texture coordinates and depths and the min/max search run in one loop in the reference where the source used
two; the clamp is one ternary store per component, ordered below one then above two hundred and fifty four; the split delta multiplies two of the plane components by 0.875
rather than a range; the return is a character; and a three-entry neighbour table replaces arithmetic on an index modulo three. Flag packing is written as one expression
whose mask order matches the reference. What remains is allocation plus one clamp path where the reference keeps the high bound in a floating register and compares stack to
register, which is recorded as the next lever with the exact instruction shape.
`0x4E5A00` moves from 122 to 171 with the object at 1991 against 2033, and its first twenty-seven bytes are now identical: four locals that the reference zeroes at entry are
initialised in the declaration block, which also fixes a resume path that read an uninitialised counter. The spill-slot assignment that follows is liveness-driven, with the
reference's slots in declaration order and this build's not, for identical live ranges, so it is reported rather than padded.

## 2026-11-03 — a dense switch that overran the extent, and a local the callee takes by address

`0x55EA30` moves from 193 to 895 matched bytes with the object landing exactly on its extent, and the largest single lever was a dispatch shape: a four-case switch compiles
to a jump table, whose sixteen bytes pushed two labels past the end of the function. The reference tests the four cases as a chain, so writing the chain takes the object back
inside the extent and raises the match by a hundred and thirty before anything else is fixed.
Four more repairs followed. The comparison multiplies a float by a double and by an integer converted to double, so the casts had to come off; the product needed parentheses so
the two floating operands multiply before the integer one, which is the reference's instruction order. An integer whose address is passed to a call needed to be a separate
local, because in the reference the counted value itself never has a memory home; that change alone added nearly four hundred matched bytes by removing four spills. Two
callees take a character parameter, so the signed extension disappears and the slot dword is pushed directly.
`0x434BA0` moves from 123 to 390 with the object at 2013 against 2053. Three findings are structural: the position, minimum and maximum vectors are four floats wide, which
makes the frame the reference's 0x48; the bounding box clamp loads both operands and selects, so it is written as two ternaries with the box first, which reproduces the
reference's parity masks; and a pointer loaded from the animation record must be reloaded per comparison because a cached local cannot alias, which the reference shows by
reloading it. The point comparisons also had to be written in negated form so that unordered results take the same branch as the reference; that change lowered the positional
count from 439 to 390 while making six branch sequences byte-identical and raising exactly-equal instructions from 60 to 84, so it was kept for correctness and both numbers
are recorded.
Both rows report an allocation remainder rather than a defect: one frame is 104 bytes larger in the reference with no code touching the gap, and the other reuses argument space
for scratch counters where a C local cannot be placed.

## 2026-11-03 — the environment reverted mid-session, and a scan that finds no more merged rows

The venv reverted from the editable checkout to the released wheel during this round without any command I ran, which announced itself the same way as before: the gap
diagnostic crashed again on the bytearray key after a repair was verified in the same environment minutes earlier. Reinstalling from the checkout with the compat editable
mode restores it, and the check that makes this visible is one line that prints the loaded module path and whether the repaired expression is present. Every measurement that
matters should be preceded by that check while a tooling repair is in flight, because a reverted environment silently measures with different code.
A scan for rows whose extent covers a second function found no further cases. The detector looked for a first-argument load followed by a stack adjustment, or a frame-pointer
prologue, at a point preceded by a return, an unconditional jump or nop padding, inside each row's own extent. It reproduces the one known case at the right offset, and it
reports no others across the store, so that split appears to have been singular rather than a class.

## 2026-11-03 — the row that spans two functions is now bounded, and its last call block is a merge wall

With the extent corrected to 1215 bytes, `0x5e5ea0` measures 344 of 1228, so the reconstruction is thirteen bytes long. The first divergence is at offset 0x112 where this
build pushes a fourth argument before a variadic call and the reference does not: the reference cleans four bytes after the inner call and lands three pushes for the outer
call, which means its compiler reused the zero it had already pushed for the variadic argument as the outer call's fourth argument. Writing the outer call with three
arguments is not possible because the translation unit's prototype declares four, and the compiler rejects it, so the reuse is a code-generation merge this toolchain does not
perform from this source.
The row is restored to that state and the finding is recorded as the last remaining difference on a function whose reconstruction is otherwise complete, rather than as a
missing piece of the body.

## 2026-11-03 — correction: the venv never reverted, two installs of the tool were in play

The earlier entry blamed a silent environment revert for the gap diagnostic crashing after a repair had been verified in the same venv. That is wrong and is corrected here.
The venv stayed on the editable checkout throughout. The crash came from a second installation: a global `uv tool` copy at `~/.local/bin/rebrew`, built from the released wheel,
which sits ahead of the project venv on `PATH`. Delegated passes that ran `rebrew` by name therefore executed released code, while the checks I ran through `.venv/bin/rebrew`
executed the checkout, and both reports were true about their own process.
Two consequences. Every delegated brief must name the absolute `.venv/bin/rebrew` path rather than saying "use the project virtual environment", because a bare command can
resolve to a different tool with different code. And the global tool is now reinstalled from the checkout, so both binaries carry the key repair and a bare command can no
longer produce the stale failure.
A separate correction concerns the row this round attacked: a diagnostic that removed only the loop-head push of the constant left the entry hoist in place, so the recorded
cause for `0x50ee80` is wrong. The body's own uses of the constant force the loop-wide register home; loop shape is not a lever, and four loop forms compiled to byte-identical
text. That row now has no open source lever at all.

`0x4E51D0` moves from 230 to 625 matched bytes with the object at 1923 against the 1953 extent, its structural ratio from 0.746 to 0.851 mnemonic and 0.518 to 0.411

different register and slot assignments. The frame, the message and both large locals already sit at the reference's offsets.

## 2026-11-03 — where the command row's thirty bytes go

The command row is thirty bytes short of its extent, and the deficit decomposes into two regions rather than a missing block. In the first, the reference pushes a buffer
address it already holds in a register where this build recomputes the address with a load-effective and pushes the new register, which costs three bytes and also moves the
zero store two slots up. In the second, the reference folds a record's base and index into one register chain before a counted copy where this build keeps the two apart, which
accounts for the rest of the shift. Both are register allocation, not missing statements, so the row cannot be closed by transcription and stays parked with its measured
numbers rather than being padded.

## 2026-11-03 — a slot record with two fields exchanged, and four constants that came from a sibling

`0x4F01C0` moves from 118 to 147 matched bytes with the object from 1697 to 1712 against the 1799 extent, whose last byte is the function's return, so the extent is one function
and not two.
Seven repairs were kept, and four of them are constants that were simply wrong: a call takes the integer two hundred where the source passed a float; another takes eighty
rather than twenty as a float; a third takes minus three rather than minus six; and a fourth takes twelve thousand two hundred rather than fifteen thousand two hundred and
thirty two. That pattern, constants that belong to a sibling row, has now appeared on three rows and is worth checking first on any row whose windows are small and scattered.
The other three are structural: a slot record had two fields exchanged at both store sites and in the replacement comparison; a four-byte record of byte fields assigned
byte-wise was declared as something else; and one message field belongs eight bytes higher. One counter assignment had to move to the top of the record loop, which was the
largest single win.

occupant cannot be identified and no dummy was added. One rejected shape widened a vector to four floats and lost sixty-eight matched bytes by moving the prologue.
